text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A quarterly board meeting. Agenda item seven: AI update. The chief technology officer has twenty slides. Slide three says forty two AI pilots are underway. Slide nine says eighty five percent of staff have used the new AI assistant. Slide fourteen has a quote from a happy customer.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the chair, who has been patient for forty minutes, asks one question. "What did it do to EBITDA?"

speaker: CLAIRE
text: And the room goes quiet.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Welcome to Talking AI to the Board and LPs, the show about telling the AI story to the people who hold you accountable for it: boards, investment committees, limited partners and, eventually, buyers. I'm Marcus.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: And I'm Claire. Over four long episodes, we're going to work through how to measure and communicate AI value and risk, honestly and convincingly. Today, the portfolio company board: what to measure, how to baseline and attribute, what a good board pack looks like, and how to talk about risk and failure. Episode two moves up to the fund: reporting AI across a whole portfolio. Episode three is limited partners: letters, annual meetings, due diligence questionnaires and fundraising, including the regulatory rules on what you can claim. And episode four is the exit story.

speaker: MARCUS
text: The usual notes. Public sources only, made-up example companies, and nothing here is investment, legal or accounting advice.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: And one promise. We're going to be hard on vanity metrics. If you've ever put "number of pilots" on a board slide, this episode is for you.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's start with that board meeting. Why does AI reporting so often go wrong?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Four reasons. First, people report what's easy to count rather than what matters. Pilots, users, logins, prompts, features shipped. Those are activity measures. A board is responsible for value and risk, and activity tells it neither.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Second.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The wrong person presents. AI updates are often given by the technology leader, because AI feels technical. But the value of AI shows up in operations, sales, finance and customer service. If the head of customer service can't tell the board what the AI phone agent did to bookings, the board is hearing about tools, not results.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Third.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: No baseline. Many AI initiatives launch without anyone measuring the before state. Six months later, the numbers look better, but nobody can say how much is the AI and how much is seasonality, a price increase, or a new manager. The board is asked to take it on faith.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And fourth?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Separate stories for value and risk. The CTO presents the exciting AI update. Three agenda items later, the general counsel presents a compliance update that mentions AI risks. The board never sees them together, so it can't weigh them. Good AI reporting puts value, risk and the plan on the same page.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the consequence?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Two bad outcomes. Either the board loses patience and cuts the AI budget, even where it was working. Or the board gets swept up in the enthusiasm and funds a lot of activity that never pays back. Both are failures of reporting, not of AI.

speaker: MARCUS
text: So where should AI reporting start?
chapter: Start from the value creation plan

speaker: CLAIRE
text: With the value creation plan. In a private equity-backed company, the board's main job is to oversee the plan that will create the return: revenue growth, margin improvement, cash generation, acquisitions, and the eventual exit. AI isn't a separate strategy. It's a set of levers inside that plan.
chapter: Start from the value creation plan

speaker: MARCUS
text: So the AI line in the plan should look like the other lines.
chapter: Start from the value creation plan

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Exactly like them. A pricing initiative has a target, an owner, a timeline and a measure. A procurement initiative does too. An AI initiative should as well. "AI-enabled after-hours call handling: target one point two million dollars of incremental gross profit in year one, owned by the head of customer operations, live across all branches by the end of the second quarter, measured by booked jobs from AI-handled calls times average gross profit per job." That's a line a board can oversee.
chapter: Start from the value creation plan

speaker: MARCUS
text: And if the plan has no AI line?
chapter: Start from the value creation plan

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Then the first step is to add one, built from the company's own data, as our Real Economy show describes. A few workflows, each with a dollar range, an owner and a time frame. Once those exist, reporting has something to report against.
chapter: Start from the value creation plan

speaker: MARCUS
text: And how many AI lines?
chapter: Start from the value creation plan

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Few. Three to five significant AI initiatives, at most, for a mid-sized company. Each big enough to matter to the plan. Everything else, the smaller experiments and productivity tools, gets reported as a group, if at all. The board doesn't need forty two pilots. It needs the five things that will move the numbers.
chapter: Start from the value creation plan

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's get into measurement. How do you choose the right measure for an AI initiative?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: I use a chain with four links. The activity, what the AI does. The operational outcome, what changes in how the work gets done. The financial outcome, what changes in the profit and loss or the balance sheet. And the evidence, how we know it was the AI. Every AI initiative should be reported along that chain, with the board's attention on the last two links.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Walk me through an example.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Take an AI voice agent in a home services company. Activity: calls answered by the AI, by hour. Operational outcome: answer rate, booking rate on AI-handled calls, cancellations of AI-booked jobs. Financial outcome: incremental booked revenue and gross profit from calls that would previously have gone to voicemail, minus the cost of the AI and any answering service it replaced. Evidence: comparison with the same hours in the prior year, and with branches that went live later.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And for a less direct one, like an AI assistant for staff?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: That's harder, and worth being honest about. Activity: share of staff using it weekly. Operational outcome: time saved on specific tasks, measured in a sample, or faster cycle times, like proposals written per week or days to close the books. Financial outcome: only if the saved time has a destination, like handling more volume without hiring, or reducing overtime or contractor spend. Evidence: the hiring plan versus volume growth, overtime trends, cycle time data.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And if there's no financial outcome?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Then say so. "This tool improves staff experience and modestly speeds up some tasks. We don't attribute EBITDA to it. It costs this much and we think it's worth it for retention and capability." Boards respect that more than an invented productivity number.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Is there a standard set of financial outcomes to report?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: I'd use four, which match the levers in our Real Economy show. Revenue captured: money the business now collects that it didn't before, like missed calls turned into jobs, denied claims recovered, quotes followed up. Cost avoided or removed: labor hours, overtime, contractors, outsourced services, or vendor costs that are lower because of AI, or growth absorbed without hiring.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the other two.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Cash released: working capital improvements, like faster invoicing, fewer disputes, lower inventory. And risk reduced: fewer defects, fewer compliance findings, fewer customer complaints, lower loss rates. The first two hit EBITDA. The third hits cash. The fourth protects value and often shows up at exit rather than in the quarter.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And you net off the costs.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Always. The software subscriptions, the AI usage charges, the integration work, the internal team's time, the training. Report AI value net of AI cost. A board that later discovers the costs were left out will discount everything else you've told it.

speaker: MARCUS
text: What about one-time costs?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Show them separately as investment, with the payback period. "We spent four hundred thousand dollars to integrate and launch. Run-rate net benefit is now ninety thousand a month. Payback in under five months." That's the language boards use for any investment, and AI should be no different.

speaker: MARCUS
text: You mentioned baselines. How do you set one properly?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Before launch, measure the outcome you expect to change, over a long enough period to be representative, ideally twelve months, so you can see seasonality. If that's not possible, at least three months, plus last year's same period. Agree the baseline with finance, and write it down. Then, after launch, report against it every month.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And attribution, separating the AI's effect from everything else?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: There are a few practical methods, in order of strength. The strongest is a controlled comparison: roll out to some sites, teams or customers first, and compare them with similar ones that haven't started yet. That's often possible, because rollouts are usually staged anyway. Plan the staging so it produces evidence.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And when that's not possible?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Then a before and after comparison, adjusted for known factors like volume, price changes and seasonality. Weaker, but useful if done carefully. And for some initiatives, direct measurement: the AI-handled calls that booked jobs are directly countable, because before the AI those calls went to voicemail. Where the counterfactual is that obvious, attribution is simple.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And what about overlapping initiatives?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: That's the common problem. AI dispatch launched the same quarter as a new pricing policy and a new branch manager. Be honest: report the combined improvement, say what share you attribute to AI and why, and give a range. And make sure the same dollar isn't counted twice, once by the pricing team and once by the AI team. Finance should own the reconciliation.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Finance owning AI value. That's a theme.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It's essential. The single biggest credibility boost for AI reporting is when the CFO stands behind the numbers. Not the vendor, not the technology team, not the consultant. Finance-validated AI value is a different category of evidence.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Financial outcomes can take months to show. What should a board look at in the meantime?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Leading indicators that predict the financial outcome. For a voice agent, the answer rate and the booking rate tell you within weeks whether revenue will follow. For AI documentation in healthcare, the share of clinicians using it for most visits predicts the time savings. For AI quoting, the quote turnaround time predicts the win rate. Choose one or two leading indicators per initiative, and report them monthly.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And adoption?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Adoption is a leading indicator, if it's defined properly. Not "has logged in once," but "uses it for the intended work, most of the time." Our Real Economy show discussed the large AI scribe study published in JAMA this year, where the clinicians who used the tool on more than half of their visits got about three times the documentation reduction, but only about a third reached that level. That's why adoption depth matters more than adoption breadth.

speaker: MARCUS
text: So "eighty five percent of staff have used the assistant" isn't useful.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It's a start, but it's breadth. Depth is "sixty percent of the target users use it on most of their eligible work, up from forty percent last quarter." That tells the board whether the value is coming.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And quality indicators?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Every AI initiative should have one quality measure, so the board can see if speed or cost is coming at the expense of quality. Error rates in AI-coded invoices. Cancellation rates on AI-booked jobs. Escalations from AI chat to humans. Customer satisfaction on AI-handled interactions. Those also double as risk indicators.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's talk about the other direction: asking the board to fund AI. How should a management team present an AI investment case?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Like any other investment case, with three AI-specific additions. The standard parts: the problem, the size of the opportunity from the company's own data, the cost, the timeline, the owner, and the payback. The first addition is a staged structure. AI initiatives carry more uncertainty than, say, a new warehouse, so ask for funding in stages with gates. A small first stage to prove the leading indicator, then a larger second stage to scale if the gate is passed.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Second addition.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: An honest range. Low, middle and high cases, with the middle case assuming realistic adoption, not perfect adoption. And say what the low case looks like, including the possibility that it doesn't work. Boards are more willing to fund a range they believe than a point estimate they doubt.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And third?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The running costs. Many AI products have usage-based pricing, so costs grow with volume. Show the cost at today's volume and at the volume in the plan, and what happens if the vendor raises prices at renewal. Boards have been surprised by AI cost growth, and showing it up front builds trust.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And how big should the asks be?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Proportionate to the value. A useful rule from our Real Economy show: the quick win should pay for itself within a year, and its results should help fund the bigger bet. If the first ask is large and the payback is long, the board is right to be cautious.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's design the board pack. What does a good AI board report look like?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: One page, with an appendix for those who want more. At the top, a summary: total net AI value delivered to date and this quarter, against plan, in dollars, split into the four value lines. Then a short table, one row per major initiative: what it is, owner, status, leading indicator, financial outcome versus target, quality measure, and a traffic light.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And below the table?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Three short sections. Risks and incidents: any AI incidents this quarter, their severity and resolution, and the top three AI risks with their status. That's where governance from our sister show, The Rulebook, feeds in. Decisions needed: anything the board needs to approve, like budget for the next initiative or a policy change. And what's next: the next one or two initiatives, with their expected value and start date.

speaker: MARCUS
text: That's a lot on one page.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It fits, if the writing is tight. And the discipline of fitting it on one page forces the team to decide what matters. The appendix can have the detail: methodology for attribution, adoption trends, the AI inventory summary, regulatory calendar.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And who presents it?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The CEO or COO owns the page, and each initiative owner speaks to their row if asked. The technology leader speaks to the platform and the risks. That way, the board hears about AI as part of running the business.

speaker: MARCUS
text: How often should AI be on the board agenda?
chapter: How often, and how much time

speaker: CLAIRE
text: For most companies, the one-page report goes in the pack every quarter, with ten to fifteen minutes of discussion, usually integrated into the value creation plan review rather than a separate agenda item. Once a year, a deeper session: strategy, the competitive picture, the disruption question, governance, and the next year's AI plan.
chapter: How often, and how much time

speaker: MARCUS
text: And for companies where AI is central?
chapter: How often, and how much time

speaker: CLAIRE
text: More. A software company whose product is AI, or a company where AI decisions are regulated, should have AI on the agenda every meeting, with a committee doing deeper work in between. That's also what the oversight duty discussion in The Rulebook suggests: when AI is mission critical, the board needs a regular system to hear about it.
chapter: How often, and how much time

speaker: MARCUS
text: And between meetings?
chapter: How often, and how much time

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A monthly dashboard to the board chair or the fund's operating partner, with the same structure as the board page. It keeps the people closest to the investment informed and avoids surprises at the board meeting.
chapter: How often, and how much time

speaker: MARCUS
text: Should management incentives be tied to AI?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: To AI outcomes, where they're material, not to AI activity. If an AI initiative is a significant part of the value creation plan, the relevant owners' annual objectives should include its financial outcome. The head of customer operations has a target for revenue from AI-handled calls. The controller has a target for days to invoice. That's just good management by objectives.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And not activity?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Never "deploy five AI tools" or "train everyone on AI." Those targets produce exactly the vanity metrics we've been criticizing. People will deploy five tools, and none of them will matter.

speaker: MARCUS
text: What about the CEO's long-term incentive?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: In private equity-backed companies, the CEO's main incentive is usually equity tied to the exit value. That already rewards AI that improves the business. Adding a specific AI component is rarely necessary. What's more useful is making sure the AI initiatives in the value creation plan are visible in the regular performance reviews, so they get attention alongside everything else.

speaker: MARCUS
text: What changes for a business with many sites, like a roll-up?
chapter: Reporting in multi-site and roll-up businesses

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Two things. First, report by site or by cohort. In a roll-up, AI initiatives usually roll out site by site, and sites joined the platform at different times. A table showing each cohort's performance before and after the AI went live, and before and after it joined the platform, is the clearest evidence of value. It also shows the board whether newer acquisitions are improving faster than older ones did, which is the core of the roll-up thesis.
chapter: Reporting in multi-site and roll-up businesses

speaker: MARCUS
text: And second?
chapter: Reporting in multi-site and roll-up businesses

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Separate the platform effect from the AI effect. In a roll-up, centralizing billing or dispatch creates value even without AI. Adding AI on top creates more. Boards and future buyers will want to know which is which, because the platform effect proves the integration capability, and the AI effect proves the operating model. Where you can't separate them cleanly, say so and give a reasoned split.
chapter: Reporting in multi-site and roll-up businesses

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the lagging sites?
chapter: Reporting in multi-site and roll-up businesses

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Name them. If three branches have low adoption of the AI dispatch tool and worse results, the board should know, along with the plan to fix it. The variation between sites is often where the most useful management conversation happens.
chapter: Reporting in multi-site and roll-up businesses

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's talk about failure. How do you report an AI initiative that isn't working?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Early, plainly, and with a decision. "Our AI quoting initiative is behind plan. Quote turnaround has improved from four days to two, but the win rate hasn't moved, and estimators are editing most of the drafts heavily. We think the drawings are more varied than the vendor's tool handles. Options: one, invest another quarter with a different configuration; two, narrow it to our three most standard product lines; three, stop. We recommend option two."

speaker: MARCUS
text: That's refreshingly direct.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It's what boards want. A board can handle bad news. What it can't handle is bad news that arrives late or wrapped in optimism. A team that reports a failing initiative clearly and recommends a decision earns credibility for every other number it reports.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And stopping things?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Normalize it. Set kill criteria at the start: if the leading indicator hasn't reached a certain level by a certain date, we stop or change course. Then the decision to stop is a pre-agreed outcome, not a personal failure. And write down what was learned, because the next initiative, or the next portfolio company, will benefit.

speaker: MARCUS
text: What about incidents, like a chatbot that said something it shouldn't?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Report them in the risks section, with what happened, the impact, how it was caught, what was fixed, and what changed in the controls. And frame it as evidence of a working system, if it was. "Our weekly review of AI calls caught a misclassification of emergency calls within three days. No customer was harmed. We updated the emergency rules and added a test." That's a good story about governance, not an embarrassment.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's do a list. Vanity metrics and what to replace them with.
chapter: Vanity metrics, and what to say instead

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Number of pilots: replace with number of initiatives in production at scale, and their net value. Number of users: replace with depth of adoption in the target group. Number of prompts or conversations: replace with outcomes per conversation, like resolution rate or booking rate. Hours saved: replace with where the hours went, like more jobs completed, lower overtime, or growth without hiring.
chapter: Vanity metrics, and what to say instead

speaker: MARCUS
text: Keep going.
chapter: Vanity metrics, and what to say instead

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Features shipped: replace with customer adoption of those features and the revenue or retention effect. Percent of code written by AI: replace with engineering throughput and quality, like cycle time from idea to release, and incident rates. Model accuracy in testing: replace with accuracy in production on real cases, and the business effect of errors. And "AI-enabled": replace with what, specifically, the AI does, and what it's worth.
chapter: Vanity metrics, and what to say instead

speaker: MARCUS
text: The code one is interesting.
chapter: Vanity metrics, and what to say instead

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It's become a popular vanity metric in software companies. "Forty percent of our code is now AI-generated." It might be true, but it says nothing about whether the company ships better software faster. Research has shown mixed effects on developer productivity, including a 2025 study by METR that found experienced developers working on their own large projects were slower with AI tools, despite believing they were faster. So measure what the board cares about: what gets shipped, how fast, and how well.
chapter: Vanity metrics, and what to say instead

speaker: MARCUS
text: You said risk should sit alongside value. What risk information does a board actually need?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Four things, briefly. The AI inventory summary: how many AI uses, how many in each risk tier, and any changes. The high-risk uses, by name, with their control status. Incidents and near misses this quarter. And the regulatory calendar: rules taking effect in the next twelve months that affect the company, and readiness for each. For a European business with high-risk uses, that's the December 2027 date under the EU AI Act. For a US business making consequential decisions about consumers, it's January 2027, when Colorado's replacement law and California's automated decision rules start.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And strategic risk?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: That's the disruption question: whether AI threatens the business model. It doesn't belong in the quarterly report, but it should be on the annual strategy agenda, with an honest view of exposure and what the company is doing about it. Our sister show, The AI Diligence Room, has a whole episode on running that test.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the risk of doing too little?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Absolutely include it. Under-adoption is a strategic risk. If competitors are using AI to answer every call, quote faster and serve customers more cheaply, a company that's cautious may lose share. A good board report makes clear both the risks of AI and the risk of not using it.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Everything so far sounds like a services business. What changes when the portfolio company sells software?
chapter: A different page for software companies

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The board page has two halves. The first is AI in the product: what customers buy. The second is AI in the company's own operations, especially engineering, support and sales. They need different measures.
chapter: A different page for software companies

speaker: MARCUS
text: Start with the product.
chapter: A different page for software companies

speaker: CLAIRE
text: For AI in the product, the board needs adoption of AI features by customers, not just availability. Revenue attributable to AI, defined carefully: separately priced AI products, AI add-ons, or the uplift in renewals and expansions where AI is the reason. Gross margin on AI features, because AI has real running costs. Net revenue retention in the segments most exposed to AI disruption. And pricing model progress, like the share of revenue moving from seats to usage or outcomes.
chapter: A different page for software companies

speaker: MARCUS
text: Why the exposed segments?
chapter: A different page for software companies

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Because the board needs an early warning on the disruption question. If seat counts are falling at renewal in customer segments where AI is reducing headcount, the board should see that trend quarter by quarter, not discover it in a bad year. That's the threat side of AI, and it belongs on the same page as the opportunity.
chapter: A different page for software companies

speaker: MARCUS
text: And AI in the company's own operations?
chapter: A different page for software companies

speaker: CLAIRE
text: For engineering: throughput and quality, like lead time from idea to release, deployment frequency, change failure rate and time to restore service, plus engineering cost as a share of revenue. For support: resolution rate by AI, customer satisfaction, and support cost per customer. For sales: pipeline coverage and sales cycle length where AI assists. And in all cases, AI costs, because software companies can spend a lot on AI tools for their own staff.
chapter: A different page for software companies

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the AI cost line?
chapter: A different page for software companies

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Show it clearly: AI costs in cost of revenue for product features, and AI costs in operating expenses for internal tools. Both trending against the value they produce. A board that sees AI costs growing faster than AI revenue for three quarters will rightly ask why, and it's better if management raises it first.
chapter: A different page for software companies

speaker: MARCUS
text: And for regulated companies, like healthcare services or insurance?
chapter: Regulated companies: value and compliance together

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The board page needs a compliance column next to every value number. In healthcare, if AI coding assistance increased revenue per visit, the board needs to see that the coding distribution has been audited and that the increase reflects accuracy, not aggressiveness. In insurance, if AI claims triage reduced cycle times, the board needs to see that outcomes don't differ unfairly across groups and that adjusters make the decisions.
chapter: Regulated companies: value and compliance together

speaker: MARCUS
text: So value without the compliance evidence is incomplete.
chapter: Regulated companies: value and compliance together

speaker: CLAIRE
text: In regulated work, it's worse than incomplete. A revenue number from AI coding without an audit result is a potential liability presented as an achievement. Our Real Economy show's healthcare episode calls it the bright line: accuracy, never aggression. The board page should show the evidence that the line is being respected, every quarter.
chapter: Regulated companies: value and compliance together

speaker: MARCUS
text: Who should present it?
chapter: Regulated companies: value and compliance together

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The business owner presents the value, and the compliance officer confirms the controls, side by side. That joint presentation tells the board that value and compliance are managed together, not traded off against each other.
chapter: Regulated companies: value and compliance together

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's run a made-up example. Ridgeline Services, the facilities services company from our Real Economy show: eighty million dollars of revenue, two thousand staff. It's six months into its AI plan. What does its board page say?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Summary line: "Net AI value delivered year to date: four hundred and ten thousand dollars of EBITDA and one point one million dollars of cash, against a plan of five hundred thousand and one million." Then the table, with three initiatives.

speaker: MARCUS
text: The first.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: AI handling of inbound client requests after hours and at lunch. Owner: head of client services. Status: live across all regions. Leading indicator: answer rate up from eighty five to ninety eight percent. Financial outcome: two hundred and sixty thousand dollars of incremental gross profit from additional paid work requests, net of AI costs. Quality: three percent of AI-handled requests escalated to staff, client satisfaction flat. Green.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Second.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: AI-assisted invoicing and contract checking. Owner: controller. Status: live. Leading indicator: days to invoice down from nine to three, disputes down from two percent to one. Financial outcome: one point one million dollars of cash released from lower receivables, plus a hundred and fifty thousand dollars of reduced credit notes and write-offs. Quality: error rate in sample audit below one percent. Green.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And third.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: AI-assisted bid writing. Owner: sales director. Status: in use for forty percent of bids. Leading indicator: bid preparation time down by a third. Financial outcome: none yet, because win rates take time to show, and the sales cycle is long. Quality: estimators report needing heavy edits on complex sites. Amber, with a decision to focus the tool on standard office sites for the next quarter.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the rest of the page?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Risks: one incident, where the client request agent quoted a price for a service Ridgeline doesn't offer in one region, caught in the weekly review, fixed by updating the service catalogue. Top risks: data quality in the scheduling system, which blocks the next initiative, and client contract terms on data use. Decision needed: approve budget for AI-assisted scheduling, the biggest opportunity, at an estimated one point five to three million dollars of annual overtime savings, starting next quarter. What's next: scheduling, then quality audits.

speaker: MARCUS
text: That's a page a chair would be happy with.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Because it answers the chair's question. What did it do to EBITDA and cash, how do we know, what's the risk, and what do you need from us.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's be honest. Sometimes the board itself makes AI reporting worse. How?
chapter: When the board is part of the problem

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Two ways, in opposite directions. Some boards push for hype. A director reads about AI, wants the company to have an AI story, and asks why there aren't more pilots. Management responds by launching more pilots, and the board gets activity reporting, because that's what it signaled it wanted. The fix is for the chair to set the expectation clearly: we want fewer initiatives, measured in dollars.
chapter: When the board is part of the problem

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the other direction?
chapter: When the board is part of the problem

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Boards that are so skeptical, or so risk-averse, that every AI proposal gets deferred. Often that's because directors don't feel equipped to judge it. The fix there is education, an annual deep-dive session, and a staged funding structure that limits the downside of saying yes. And sometimes an outside view: a fund operating partner or an advisor who has seen the same initiative work at other companies.
chapter: When the board is part of the problem

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the fund's role on the board?
chapter: When the board is part of the problem

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The fund's representatives usually set the tone. If they ask "what did it do to EBITDA, and how do we know," management will report that way. If they ask "what's our AI story," management will produce stories. The questions directors ask shape the reporting they get.
chapter: When the board is part of the problem

speaker: MARCUS
text: Practically, who puts the AI board report together, and how?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: In a mid-sized company, one person in the finance or strategy team owns the AI value report, the same person who tracks the rest of the value creation plan. Each initiative owner provides their numbers monthly in a standard template: leading indicator, operational outcome, financial outcome with method, quality measure, and issues. Finance reconciles the financial outcomes against the accounts. The AI governance lead provides the risk section.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the data?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Automate where you can. Most of the leading indicators come from systems: the phone system, the field service platform, the billing system, the AI vendor's logs. A simple dashboard that pulls those monthly saves hours and reduces arguments about the numbers. But keep a human review step, because automated numbers can be wrong in ways nobody notices until a director asks.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And how long should it take?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Once the machine is set up, a day or two a month. If it takes a week, the template is too complicated. And the same monthly data feeds the fund's portfolio reporting, which is next episode's topic, so it's worth getting the structure right once.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's talk about the mechanics of the meeting itself, because a good report can still go badly in the room.
chapter: The pre-read and the meeting itself

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The most important piece is the pre-read. Board members should get the one-page AI report, plus any backup, several days before the meeting, so the meeting is for questions and decisions rather than for reading slides together. If the first time the board sees the numbers is when they're on the screen, you'll spend the whole slot explaining definitions.
chapter: The pre-read and the meeting itself

speaker: MARCUS
text: And who presents?
chapter: The pre-read and the meeting itself

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The CEO should introduce the item in a sentence or two, to show it's a business priority and not a technology side project. Then the person who owns the work presents, briefly. And the chief financial officer should be visibly comfortable with the numbers. If the CFO looks uneasy when the AI savings figure comes up, every experienced director will notice, and they'll discount the figure.
chapter: The pre-read and the meeting itself

speaker: MARCUS
text: How long should the presentation part be?
chapter: The pre-read and the meeting itself

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Five minutes, maybe less. Highlights, what changed since last quarter, any decision needed. The rest of the slot is questions. If management is talking for twenty minutes, the report isn't doing its job.
chapter: The pre-read and the meeting itself

speaker: MARCUS
text: What about the decision itself? Boards often leave the AI item without having decided anything.
chapter: The pre-read and the meeting itself

speaker: CLAIRE
text: That's a common failure. Every AI item should end with one of three outcomes: the board notes progress and no decision is needed; the board approves something specific, like funding for the next phase or a change of target; or the board asks for something specific by a date, like a deeper review of one initiative. Write it in the minutes. That creates a record of oversight, which matters for governance, and it makes next quarter's conversation easier, because you start by reporting on what the board asked for.
chapter: The pre-read and the meeting itself

speaker: MARCUS
text: And between meetings?
chapter: The pre-read and the meeting itself

speaker: CLAIRE
text: For most companies, nothing formal is needed between meetings, but two exceptions are worth agreeing in advance. A material AI incident, like a data leak or a customer harmed by an automated decision, should go to the chair quickly, with an agreed threshold for what counts as material. And a significant change in the plan, like a big initiative being stopped or a large unplanned cost, should be flagged before the next meeting rather than revealed in the pack.
chapter: The pre-read and the meeting itself

speaker: MARCUS
text: What about board education? Some directors are uneasy with the subject.
chapter: The pre-read and the meeting itself

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A short session once a year helps, ideally practical rather than theoretical: what the company's AI systems actually do, a demonstration, and the main risks. Board members don't need to understand how models work. They need enough familiarity to ask good questions and to tell a strong answer from a weak one. Some boards also add a director with operating experience in AI or digital transformation, which can help, as long as that person doesn't become the only one who engages with the topic.
chapter: The pre-read and the meeting itself

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's flip it. If you're a director receiving an AI report, what should you ask?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Seven questions. Is this number validated by finance? What's the baseline, and how did you attribute the change to AI? What did it cost, including internal time? Where did the saved time go? What's the quality measure, and is it holding? What would make you stop this? And what are we not doing with AI that our competitors are?

speaker: MARCUS
text: Any red flags in the answers?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Numbers that come from the vendor. Savings without a destination. No quality measure. Initiatives that have been "nearly ready to scale" for three quarters. And reluctance to name an owner. Each of those suggests the value is less solid than the slide implies.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And green flags?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A CFO who can explain the methodology. Initiative owners from the business, not technology. Staged rollouts producing comparisons. Candid reporting of what isn't working. And a short list, not a long one.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Some quick questions. Should AI value be reported separately from the rest of the value creation plan?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Integrated, with a subtotal. Each AI initiative sits within its part of the plan, under revenue growth, margin or cash, and the AI page gives a subtotal so the board can see the total contribution. Separating it completely makes AI feel like a side project.

speaker: MARCUS
text: How precise do the numbers need to be?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Precise in method, honest in range. A board doesn't need two decimal places. It needs to know the number is built properly and roughly right. Round sensibly, give ranges where attribution is uncertain, and show the method in the appendix.

speaker: MARCUS
text: What if the vendor provides a dashboard with value figures?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Use it as an input, not as the answer. Vendor dashboards often count value generously, like counting every AI-handled call as revenue captured, even ones that would have been answered anyway. Have finance rebuild the number from the company's own data.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And what if we've only just started?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Then report the plan, the baselines, the leading indicators and the first results, and say plainly that financial outcomes will follow in a stated number of months. A board will wait for results it was told to expect. It won't wait for results that keep being promised without dates.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Sum it up.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Start from the value creation plan, and give each major AI initiative a line like any other initiative: target, owner, timeline, measure. Keep it to three to five significant initiatives.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Measurement?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Report along the chain: activity, operational outcome, financial outcome, evidence, with attention on the last two. Use four value lines: revenue captured, cost removed, cash released and risk reduced, always net of AI cost. Set baselines before launch, use staged rollouts for attribution, and have finance validate the numbers. Track depth of adoption and a quality measure.

speaker: MARCUS
text: The board pack?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: One page: summary, initiative table, risks and incidents, decisions needed, what's next. Presented by the business, not just technology. Report failures early with a recommended decision, and set kill criteria up front. Replace vanity metrics with outcomes. And put value and risk on the same page, including the risk of doing too little.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Next time: moving up a level, to the fund. How to report AI across a whole portfolio.
